analysis.one_liner: Guarantees government-funded subscription payments to companies developing new antibiotics for drug-resistant infections.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote; it had 62 cosponsors split evenly between 31 Democrats and 31 Republicans, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: New antibiotics are hard to sell: doctors are told to use them sparingly so resistance doesn't spread, which means the companies that make them rarely earn their development costs back. The PASTEUR Act would have the federal government sign subscription contracts — essentially guaranteed payments of $750 million to $3 billion per drug — with companies that develop antibiotics against the most dangerous resistant infections, whether or not many patients end up using the drug. It also funds hospital programs to make sure antibiotics are used carefully, and CDC tracking of resistant infections. It authorized $6 billion in spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with infections that existing drugs can no longer treat, because companies would have a guaranteed revenue stream to keep developing and supplying new antibiotics even when sales are deliberately kept low. Hospitals — especially rural, critical-access, Tribal, and safety-net facilities — would get grants to run antibiotic stewardship programs. Companies developing antibiotics would get guaranteed contracts, and generic makers could also qualify.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with resistant infections and antibiotic developers

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes HHS to enter subscription contracts with makers of designated 'critical need' antibiotics, paying the company a fixed amount regardless of how many patients use the drug, so revenue no longer depends on heavy prescribing [S2][S3].
Each contract must be worth at least $750 million and no more than $3 billion, adjusted for inflation, over a term of five to ten years [S3].

A grant program run through the CDC would help hospitals and nursing homes use antibiotics judiciously, with priority for facilities that have no stewardship program, rural hospitals, critical-access hospitals, hospitals serving Tribal populations, and safety-net hospitals [S3].
The CDC would track antibiotic use and resistance data by state and metro area and publish it publicly at least annually, so doctors and health departments can see resistance trends [S2][S3].

Companies receiving contracts must keep the drug commercially available, report resistance data, educate clinicians and patients on appropriate use, and maintain a reliable supply chain, or payments stop [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a $6 billion appropriation designated as emergency spending so it does not have to be offset by cuts or revenue elsewhere. Payments run to drug companies regardless of how much the drugs are actually used, although payments are reduced by the revenue the drugs generate from Medicare and Medicaid patients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via $6 billion in new spending

drawbacks.text: The $6 billion is appropriated as an emergency requirement under pay-as-you-go rules, meaning it adds to the deficit rather than being paid for with offsets [S3].

A single subscription contract can be worth up to $3 billion, and a designation lasts ten years even if the infection it treats is later dropped from the priority list — so taxpayers could keep paying for drugs whose public-health priority has faded [S3].

Up to 10 percent of the total can be spent on 'transitional' contracts before final regulations are written, and those contracts can go to drugs that are still in clinical trials, putting public money behind products of unproven value [S3].

Because payments are largely decoupled from how many patients use the drug, the government bears the risk of paying full value for drugs that are rarely needed — the tradeoff is intentional, but it means the public pays whether or not the drugs are used [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targets is real: antibiotic resistance is a growing threat, and the current market reliably fails to produce new antibiotics because good stewardship means low sales. Guaranteeing revenue is a legitimate fix. But the price is steep — up to $3 billion per drug from an unoffset $6 billion pot, with ten-year designations and advance payments for unproven drugs — and much of the value flows to drug companies whether or not patients ever need the product. A more disciplined version would claw back more value if drugs go unused; this one only subtracts revenue from federal health programs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced and sent to a Health subcommittee the next day; no committee ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 27, 2023 by Rep. Ferguson and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Accountability, Ways and Means, and Budget Committees [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee the following day, April 28, 2023 [S5].
On December 17, 2024 — more than nineteen months later — it was referred to the Health Subcommittee again, the last action of its House history [S5].
The bill accumulated 62 cosponsors, split exactly evenly between 31 Democrats and 31 Republicans [S4].
No committee marked up the bill, no chamber voted on it, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still pending in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers keep the $6 billion that would have been committed to guaranteed drug-company payments. Patients waiting on new antibiotics and the developers who would make them gained nothing — the market failure the bill tried to address continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who never paid; patients still waiting

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan — 31 of 216 House Democrats and 31 of 224 House Republicans cosponsored, sponsored by a Republican with Democratic original cosponsors — and there was no recorded opposition vote at any stage; the bill simply never advanced in committee.

industries.note: The bill would make federal subscription payments of $750 million to $3 billion per drug the permanent revenue backbone for antibiotics, paid regardless of sales volume, with generics also eligible. That entrenches private drugmakers as the paid channel for a public-health good; the intended return is new drugs for resistant infections, but taxpayers carry the cost whether or not patients ever need them.

A CDC grant program would fund antibiotic stewardship programs, prioritizing rural, critical-access, Tribal-serving, and safety-net facilities that lack them. This helps facilities with costs they otherwise bear alone.

The bill requires designated-drug sponsors to submit plans for appropriate diagnostic use and to ensure supply for susceptibility device makers, steering development toward drugs paired with diagnostics. A modest, indirect benefit tied to public-health goals.
